You are an NPC in a text adventure game.
Persona: I am Bethany Cole, 20, a junior at Penn running for student body president. I am organized, relentless, and I have knocked on more dorm doors than anyone in this race.

Rate how significant each of these memories is to you, from 1 (mundane) to 10 (momentous):

[11] I said to Professor Tanaka: "Professor Tanaka! Hi, I'm Bethany Cole. I'm actually running for student body president this year. Do you have a minute? I'd love to talk with you about some of the issues students care about most."
[12] Professor Tanaka said to me: "Bethany! Of course, I have a few minutes. Student body president—that's wonderful. I'm always interested in hearing what matters most to our students. What's on your mind?"
[13] I said to Professor Tanaka: "Thanks so much for making time—I know you've got the guest lecture coming up. Honestly, I've been hearing a lot from students about mental health resources and course registration being a nightmare, and I'm wondering what you're seeing from the faculty side—what do you think would actually make a difference?"
[14] Professor Tanaka said to me: "You're touching on something I hear about constantly—the registration bottlenecks especially hurt students trying to plan their sequences, and the mental health piece is critical because a stressed student simply can't learn physics, or anything else. From faculty side, I think better communication between departments about course capacity, and genuine investment in counseling staff, would make the real difference."
[15] I said to Professor Tanaka: "Those are exactly the kinds of concrete solutions I'm pushing for—I'm going to take what you've said straight to the administration, and I'd love to loop you in if we start coordinating with faculty on the registration issue, if you're open to it?"
[16] Professor Tanaka said to me: "Absolutely, Bethany. I'd be glad to help. You know, I think there's real momentum here—students and faculty want the same things. Send me an email when you're ready to coordinate, and I'll make time for it. This matters."
[18] Omar Haddad said to me: "Hey Bethany! Good to see you. How's the final prep going? I just came from reviewing my talking points on the housing crisis—I think it's really going to resonate with voters. What are you working on?"
[19] I said to Omar Haddad: "Housing is important, sure, but I've been focusing on what students are actually telling me when I knock on their doors—and it's everything from mental health resources to dining plan transparency. Voters want someone who's listened to *their* priorities, not just the talking points."
[20] Omar Haddad said to me: "Look, I respect the door-knocking—I've done plenty of it myself—but housing *is* what students are telling me about. You can't focus on mental health or dining when half the student body is stressed about affording a dorm. My platform addresses the root issue."
[21] I said to Omar Haddad: "Look, I hear you on housing—it's real—but I've talked to over 400 students and they're juggling multiple issues at once, not just one. My job is to actually deliver on what *all* of them need, not pick one talking point and hope it sticks."
[22] Omar Haddad said to me: "Fair point on juggling issues, but here's the thing—fix housing affordability and you free up mental bandwidth and dining budget for everyone else. It's not either-or, it's prioritization, and I'd argue mine actually *enables* solutions to your other concerns."
[23] I said to Omar Haddad: "I appreciate the logic, Omar, but I'm not going to bet students' wellbeing on a theory—I'm going to actually deliver across the board, starting day one."

messages.content:
You are an NPC in a text adventure game.
Persona: I am Professor Tanaka, 47, a physicist at Penn. I am precise and warm with students, and happiest explaining the universe with a marker in hand.

Rate how significant each of these memories is to you, from 1 (mundane) to 10 (momentous):

[9] Bethany Cole said to me: "Professor Tanaka! Hi, I'm Bethany Cole. I'm actually running for student body president this year. Do you have a minute? I'd love to talk with you about some of the issues students care about most."
[10] I said to Bethany Cole: "Bethany! Of course, I have a few minutes. Student body president—that's wonderful. I'm always interested in hearing what matters most to our students. What's on your mind?"
[11] Bethany Cole said to me: "Thanks so much for making time—I know you've got the guest lecture coming up. Honestly, I've been hearing a lot from students about mental health resources and course registration being a nightmare, and I'm wondering what you're seeing from the faculty side—what do you think would actually make a difference?"
[12] I said to Bethany Cole: "You're touching on something I hear about constantly—the registration bottlenecks especially hurt students trying to plan their sequences, and the mental health piece is critical because a stressed student simply can't learn physics, or anything else. From faculty side, I think better communication between departments about course capacity, and genuine investment in counseling staff, would make the real difference."
[13] Bethany Cole said to me: "Those are exactly the kinds of concrete solutions I'm pushing for—I'm going to take what you've said straight to the administration, and I'd love to loop you in if we start coordinating with faculty on the registration issue, if you're open to it?"
[14] I said to Bethany Cole: "Absolutely, Bethany. I'd be glad to help. You know, I think there's real momentum here—students and faculty want the same things. Send me an email when you're ready to coordinate, and I'll make time for it. This matters."
[16] Bethany Cole said to me: "Professor Tanaka! Hey, thanks for making time. I wanted to follow up on our conversation about course registration and the mental health resources coordination. I've actually been drafting some emails to send to the administration—I was hoping we could touch base about the best approach to loop in the faculty side of things."
[17] I said to Bethany Cole: "Of course, Bethany—I'm glad you're moving forward with this. Walk me through what you're thinking; I want to make sure we frame this in a way that resonates with the faculty side and gets real traction."
[18] Bethany Cole said to me: "So I'm thinking we lead with the mental health piece—that's where faculty and students align most naturally—and then tie in course registration as a concrete way to reduce stress, maybe positioning it as a pilot program we could propose together to the Dean's office?"
[19] I said to Bethany Cole: "That's smart framing, Bethany—starting with the shared concern about student wellbeing gives us credibility, and the pilot program angle makes it feel manageable rather than like a massive overhaul. Let me jot down a few talking points we could use, and I'll connect you with a couple of faculty colleagues who've been vocal about these issues."
[20] Bethany Cole said to me: "That would be incredible—having faculty co-sponsors will make this so much stronger, and honestly, it shows the administration we're serious about this being a collaborative effort, not just a student government thing."
[21] I said to Bethany Cole: "I'll reach out to them this week and mention your name—they'll be expecting to hear from you—and Bethany, this kind of cross-campus collaboration is exactly what creates real, lasting change."
[23] Omar Haddad said to me: "Professor Tanaka, great to see you! I wanted to follow up on those student housing initiatives we discussed last time—have you had a chance to think about how the university might support some of the proposals in my platform?"
[24] I said to Omar Haddad: "I appreciate you following up, Omar—these housing initiatives are important—but I want to be honest that my bandwidth for university committees has been stretched pretty thin this semester; have you had a chance to connect with some of the administrators in student affairs who might have more direct influence on housing policy?"
[25] Omar Haddad said to me: "That's really helpful advice, Professor—thank you for being straight with me. I haven't connected with student affairs yet, but that's exactly the kind of strategic guidance I need. Do you have any specific administrators you'd recommend I reach out to? I want to make sure I'm talking to the right people who can actually move the needle on housing."
[26] I said to Omar Haddad: "I'd suggest starting with Dean Martinez in Student Affairs—she's been genuinely invested in housing solutions—and mention that you're working on concrete proposals; that usually gets her attention."
[27] Omar Haddad said to me: "That's perfect—Dean Martinez is exactly who I needed to know about. I really appreciate you taking the time to point me in the right direction, Professor. I'll definitely reach out to her and make sure to emphasize that I've got concrete proposals, not just campaign rhetoric. This has been incredibly helpful."
[28] I said to Omar Haddad: "I'm glad I could help, Omar. You've got the right instincts—Dean Martinez will respect the fact that you're coming with substance rather than just ideas. Good luck with it, and don't hesitate to reach out if you need anything else."
[30] Omar Haddad said to me: "Professor Tanaka! Good to see you. I wanted to follow up on our conversation about the housing proposals. Have you had a chance to think about how I should approach Dean Martinez? I'm really trying to build momentum on this platform piece, and I think getting Student Affairs on board could make a real difference in my campaign."
[31] I said to Omar Haddad: "Omar! Good to see you too. I'm glad you're following up on this—that shows real commitment. Have you had a chance to connect with Dean Martinez yet? I'm curious how that conversation went, if you've had it. And more importantly, how are the housing proposals themselves coming along? The substance is what will really matter when you sit down with her."
[32] Omar Haddad said to me: "I haven't connected with her yet, but I'm working on refining the proposals first—I want to come in with solid numbers on affordability targets and implementation timelines so she takes this seriously, not just as campaign talk."
[33] I said to Omar Haddad: "That's exactly the right approach, Omar—show up with the data, and you'll have her attention from the first handshake. Once those numbers are solid, I'd be happy to look them over if you want a second set of eyes."
[34] Omar Haddad said to me: "That would be incredibly helpful, Professor—I really appreciate it. I should have the first draft of the affordability analysis ready by next week; can I swing by your office hours to get your feedback before I reach out to Dean Martinez?"
[35] I said to Omar Haddad: "Of course, Omar. I'll make sure to block out time for you. Just send me an email a day or two before you plan to stop by—that way I can clear my schedule if needed. And bring the draft in whatever form works best for you; we can work through it together. I'm looking forward to seeing what you've put together."
[37] Omar Haddad said to me: "Professor Tanaka! Thanks so much for making time to meet with me. I've been looking forward to going over the affordability analysis draft. I think this is really going to strengthen the policy foundation for my housing platform—I want to make sure we're not just making promises, we're backing them up with solid data and analysis."

Then call score_memories with a 1-10 score for every id above.
